issues.text: Key is correct (c) and option d is still wrong, but the new explanation for d is literally false: DonHang.Domain.csproj uses Microsoft.NET.Sdk with ImplicitUsings enabled, whose default namespaces include System.Net.Http (refs dotnet-docs core/project-sdk/overview.md:148), so HTTP types such as HttpRequestMessage are available. What the project lacks is ASP.NET Core's request types. The lesson itself only says the service 'does not know that HTTP exists', which is fine.
issues.quote: C# allows it; the Domain project simply has no HTTP types available, by design.
issues.fix: en d: "C# allows it; `OrderService` simply uses no HTTP types, by design." vi d: "C# cho phép; chỉ là `OrderService` cố ý không dùng kiểu HTTP nào."

issues.text: The diagram sends 'Order, or an exception' back to the controller, and section 3 says turning the exception into a 400 is 'someone else's job'. Only in section 5 do I learn it is the middleware, not the controller. Until then I wondered whether the controller catches the exception.
issues.quote: Turning the result into JSON, or the exception into a `400`, is someone else's job.
issues.fix: Replace "someone else's job" with "the job of the HTTP side: the controller for the result, the exception-handling middleware for the exception".

issues.text: Explanation c is still hard to parse ('would matter when the service were unreachable otherwise'); I re-read it twice. Same, milder, in b ('when every caller were'). The idea is fine; the grammar gets in the way.
issues.quote: Going through HTTP would matter when the service were unreachable otherwise, but the business layer exists so any program can call it.
issues.fix: Keep 'when' but simplify, e.g. c: 'Calling the endpoint makes sense only when a program cannot reach the service; the job can call `CancelOrderAsync` directly.' b: 'Status codes help only when every caller is an HTTP client; the nightly job is not.'
